papers.title: Are carbohydrate ring distortions determined by biology or crystallography? The impact of experimental conditions on structural data
papers.abstract: Carbohydrates are essential molecules involved in a wide range of biological processes. While their structural representation in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) has been hindered due to their highly diverse and flexible nature, advancements on X-ray crystallography and CryoEM are accelerating the obtaining of their experimental structures, which in turn supports improved analyses of their structural properties, such as the role of their non-chair conformations on biological processes. In this context, the current work provides a comprehensive and up to date overview of carbohydrate structures within the PDB through classification, quantification, and characterization of monosaccharides and glycan chains, incorporating Cremer-Pople puckering coordinates to evaluate pyranose conformations. Our findings show that, even with a steep increase in CryoEM structures including more complex oligosaccharides, carbohydrate data remains concentrate dinsmallglycanchains, with a about 4% of non-chair conformation sintopresolution structures. Free energy landscapes for the pyranose ring in the presence and absence of nine different binding proteins, including both enzymes and non-enzymes, reinforce the preferred stability of chairs and the rarity of conformational induction upon binding.

papers.title: Danuglipron and orforglipron engage GLP-1R through materially different interfaces: an unbiased molecular dynamics study
papers.abstract: GLP-1R is among the most heavily pursued targets in metabolic disease, but its natural agonist is a 30-residue peptide that must be injected. Two oral non-peptide agonists have reached late-stage trials. Cryo-EM studies have already shown that danuglipron and CHU-128, a close analogue of orforglipron, occupy the receptor differently, but not how either interface behaves over time. We ran 500 ns of unbiased all-atom molecular dynamics on GLP-1R bound to GLP-1, danuglipron (PF-06882961) and orforglipron (LY3502970), one trajectory each, in a POPC bilayer with the G protein removed. Although CHU-128 has been simulated before, its analogue, orforglipron, has not. Scored against contacts computed from the deposited structures, under a force field that shares no parameters with previous oral agonist studies, we recovered 80%, 86% and 79% above 50% occupancy. Indexing contact by chemical group, rather than by receptor residue, and normalising by molecular size, separates the two oral compounds: orforglipron carries ring systems dedicated almost entirely to one receptor domain, one of them directing 99.7% of its contact to the extracellular domain, whereas every group of danuglipron engages both. Danuglipron is correspondingly the outlier on measures that do not depend on a chosen threshold: only 33% of its contacts exceed 90% occupancy against 72% and 84%, and it is the only system whose occupancies remain unconverged at 100 ns. With single trajectories, these are observations rather than tested claims, but two drugs of the same class and comparable size occupy this receptor in structurally distinct ways.

papers.title: 4D confocal microscopy of time dependent cell and nuclear osmotic response reveals differential osmoregulation and transport kinetics
papers.abstract: A cell's ability to maintain its volume is a prerequisite for its essential physiological functions. Changes in extracellular osmolarity induce the flux of water and solutes across the cell and nuclear membrane and, therefore, alters cell and nuclear volumes. Here, we investigated the equilibrium and dynamic volumetric responses of cells and nuclei in adherent human hepatoma (HepG2) cell monolayers using live three-dimensional imaging. Through image segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and volume rendering, precise cell and nuclear volumes were quantified. We found that during hypoosmotic stress, cells swell and lose osmolytes through active volume regulation, and nuclei undergo greater relative expansion than cells. During hyperosmotic stress, we found that both cells and nuclei shrink rapidly, develop irregular morphologies and undergo passive volume regulation. Furthermore, we explored the osmotic responses in these cells by restoring isosmotic conditions following osmotic stress and found that nuclei returned to volumes greater than their initial isosmotic volume, whereas cytoplasmic volume returned to a value below its initial isosmotic volume following swelling. By fitting coupled transport models water and solute permeability estimates for both cells and nuclei were made from their dynamic responses to different anisosmotic media with and without the presence of permeating solutes dimethyl sulfoxide and ethylene glycol. Together, these quantitative measurements of cell, cytoplasm, and nuclear volumetric responses and associated transport parameters have important implications for understanding cell physiology and the mechanism of osmoregulation.

papers.title: Mechanophenotype of synovial fibroblasts correlates with patients' pathotypes and treatment response in Rheumatoid Arthritis
papers.abstract: The mechanical features of synovial fibroblasts may encode clinically relevant information for the management of rheumatoid arthritis. Indeed, it remains poorly understood the links between cellular and microenvironment mechanics with patient stratification and therapeutic response. Here we show that combining organotypic synovial cultures with multimodal mechanophenotyping and transcriptomics identifies distinct ''soft'' and ''stiff'' fibroblast states. Healthy and rheumatoid arthritis fibroblasts were cultured in two or three dimensions (organotypic cell cultures), alone or with endothelial cells, and characterized by high-throughput nanoindentation, picobalance measurements, digital holographic microscopy, Brillouin microscopy and RNA sequencing. Three-dimensional culture reduced single-cell Young's modulus and total mass while increasing dry-mass surface density; endothelial co-culture increased fibroblast stiffness and the longitudinal modulus of intact organotypic cultures. Stiffness-based grouping revealed transcriptional programmes related to extracellular-matrix remodelling, cytoskeletal contractility, and TGF-beta, WNT, and Hippo signalling. Mapping these signatures to publicly available rheumatoid arthritis clinical transcriptomic datasets associated the ''stiff'' state with fibrotic and myeloid-fibrotic pathotypes and treatment-refractory programmes, whereas the ''soft'' state aligned with lymphoid pathotypes and rituximab- or tocilizumab-responsive programmes. These findings support mechanophenotype-associated transcriptional signatures as potential biomarkers for rheumatoid arthritis stratification.

papers.title: bioRheoFlow A Rheometric Platform for In Situ Biofilm Mechanics Under Controlled Flow Conditions
papers.abstract: Biofilm mechanics depend strongly on growth history, hydration, nutrient availability, and interfacial attachment, yet conventional rheology requires harvesting and transfer that can perturb the as-grown structure. Here, we introduce bioRheoFlow, a 3D-printed rheometer-mounted platform for cultivation and mechanical characterization without sample transfer. The platform combines evaporation compensation with static or axial nutrient flow, and benchmark measurements validate its rheometric performance. Applied to Pseudomonas putida and Pantoea sp., bioRheoFlow reveals that biofilms cultivated in situ under axial flow exhibit substantially higher elastic moduli than conventionally grown and scraped samples. Despite similar linear-viscoelastic stress ranges, the species show distinct nonlinear responses: P. putida exhibits a lower crossover stress and more abrupt failure, whereas Pantoea sp. sustains larger stresses and deformations. Creep suggests contributions from bulk deformation and biofilm-substrate interactions. bioRheoFlow provides a controlled framework for probing growth-conditioned mechanics in living biofilms.

papers.title: Electrode-Tethered DNA: Interfacial Mechanics and Switching Dynamics from Ensemble-Level Atomistic Simulations
papers.abstract: Surface-tethered DNA, anchored to gold by the late 1990s, has matured into a versatile platform for biosensing, computing and actuation. Whereas the molecular behavior of DNA in bulk solution is well characterized, that of DNA at electrode interfaces remains far less understood. Here we investigate the mechanics and dynamics of electrode-tethered double-stranded DNA across surface chemistries, salt concentrations and applied potentials. Using GPU-accelerated all-atom molecular dynamics, we sample trajectory ensembles totaling 144 s over 620 simulations. The simulations reproduce key experimental observations yet uncover molecular behavior that had gone unnoticed despite nearly three decades of research. Ensemble statistics reveal a preferred orientation about the helical axis upon surface contact. Energetic analysis identifies a substantial role for Onsager-Samaras-type repulsion in opposing that contact. By reproducing experimental trends while resolving their molecular origins, these ensembles substantially narrow the longstanding simulation-experiment gap and provide a basis for engineering tethered-DNA devices.

papers.title: Metabolic cost sets the shear stress profile of optimal vascular trees
papers.abstract: Vascular remodeling responds to local wall shear stress, but transport efficiency belongs to the network as a whole. We connect these scales by minimizing dissipation under a fixed maintenance budget, with vessel cost proportional to mass raised to an exponent b. At an optimum, dissipated power is proportional to vessel cost. This yields the shear set point |{tau} | {propto} r^(b-1){ell}^(b-1)/2 for radius r and length {ell}, with uniform shear recovered at b = 1. The associated local adaptation rule decreases the global functional, although the topology it reaches retains a memory of development. Simulations with 400 and 700 sinks show that staged growth improves transport mainly by allowing pruned connections to regrow. Fluctuating demand sustains loops without increasing the maintenance budget. The local condition fixes allocation on a given support, whereas growth and variable demand shape the topology that survives.

papers.title: Polyglutamine aggregation proceeds by stochastic nucleation in the C. elegans nervous system
papers.abstract: Fibrillar protein aggregation is the hallmark of a wide variety of neurodegenerative diseases. It is still poorly understood how soluble proteins transition to fibrillar aggregates, in particular within the complex environment of cells and tissues. Here, we employ the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of polyglutamine aggregation in the nervous system of a multicellular animal. By using fluorescence microscopy in combination with mathematical modelling, we find that polyglutamine aggregation occurs by stochastic nucleation in individual neurons, at a rate that is of the same order of magnitude as previously determined for muscle cells. The J-protein DNAJB6 strongly suppresses polyglutamine aggregation in both tissues, consistent with a mechanism in which aggregation is limited by primary nucleation. We confirm that the same mechanism holds true for a construct including the disease-relevant flanking regions of Huntingtin exon 1. Altogether, our data reveal that polyglutamine aggregation occurs spontaneously and largely independent of the cellular context.

papers.title: Torque-optimized body morphing enables rapid surface to underwater diving in whirligig beetles
papers.abstract: Known for their rapid water surface locomotion, whirligig beetles (Gyrinidae) are also fast divers. They can transition from the surface to underwater swimming in under 100 ms. Diving requires them to generate sufficient hydrodynamic torque to break the water surface and reorient the body. However, the mechanism by which whirligigs create the necessary pitch-down torque is unknown. Here, we show that their diving is achieved by bending the abdomen. The inertial hydrodynamic pressure on the flexed abdomen generates the torque necessary for surface breaking and body rotation. The torque is maximized at an abdominal angle of 45{degrees}, whereas for effective diving, whirligigs display a preferential abdominal angle of around 28{degrees}, closely aligning with the angle that maximizes the torque-to-drag ratio. This abdominal angle is optimized by balancing torque generation with the drag penalty. Our findings inspire a mechanism for surface-to-underwater transition, offering design principles for multimodal robots capable of locomotion across the air-water interface.

papers.title: A Kiss-and-Ride Mechanism for Lipid Exchange at Membrane Contact Sites
papers.abstract: Lipid transfer proteins (LTPs) mediate non-vesicular lipid transport at membrane contact sites, yet how transient membrane tethering contributes to lipid transfer remains poorly understood. Here, we use the single-domain yeast phosphatidylserine transporter Osh6, a member of the oxysterol-binding protein-related protein family, to investigate tethering-dependent lipid transport. We show that Osh6 can access two transport modes depending on membrane composition: conventional shuttling between membranes and a tethering-dependent mode in which the opposing membrane facilitates cargo extraction from the donor membrane. Combining lipid transport and membrane-tethering measurements with kinetic analysis, lipid partitioning, and in vivo complementation, we provide evidence for a transient membrane-bridged intermediate during lipid transfer. Productive phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) extraction destabilizes this bridged state, allowing cargo-loaded Osh6 to disengage and continue the transport cycle. We term this mechanism kiss-and-ride, in which transient membrane contact facilitates cargo extraction ("kiss") before the cargo-loaded protein disengages ("ride"). Consistent with this model, PI4P transport is preserved in a lidless Osh6 mutant with impaired membrane dissociation, whereas phosphatidylserine transport is strongly reduced, revealing distinct mechanistic requirements for the two cargoes. Together, our findings reveal a tethering-dependent transport mode in a cup-like LTP and suggest that membrane contact sites can actively shape the mechanism of lipid transport rather than merely bringing donor and acceptor membranes into proximity.

papers.title: State-selective nanobodies to probe Guanylate-binding protein coat assembly and function
papers.abstract: Cell-autonomous immunity against gram-negative bacterial pathogens relies on Guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs). GBPs are interferon-inducible guanosine triphosphate hydrolases that coat cytosolic bacteria and promote non-canonical inflammasome activation. GBP coat assembly is initiated by GBP1, which binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide and recruits further paralogs in a hierarchical and nucleotide-dependent manner. Dissecting the contributions of individual GBPs has remained challenging because the seven human paralogs are structurally similar and undergo nucleotide-driven conformational changes that are difficult to resolve in cellular and biochemical experiments. Here, we developed a nanobody toolbox for the state-selective probing of human GBP coat assembly. We identify eight nanobodies with distinct paralog, domain, and conformational specificities and define their binding profiles and epitopes using complementary biophysical assays and cryogenic electron microscopy. We further demonstrate the utility of selected nanobodies by demonstrating their functionality in membrane reconstitution assays and in infected cells. A dimer-disrupting nanobody blocks progression of GBP-coat assembly from soluble GBP1 assemblies to LPS-associated coats, suggesting a stage-specific structural transition during coat formation. In contrast, a dimer selective nanobody binds assembled coats without measurably perturbing their organisation and is robustly recruited to GBP1-positive bacteria in infected cells, indicating that this dimer interface remains intact and accessible in coat-associated GBP1. Together, these nanobodies establish a set of state-selective reagents to distinguish, perturb, and probe GBP assemblies in structural and cellular studies.

papers.title: Red states modulate energy localization between the antenna and trap in PSI
papers.abstract: The core antenna of the photosystem I (PSI) complex of oxygenic photosynthesis operates at near perfect quantum efficiency, making it one of the most efficient energy conversation devices in nature. The presence of low energy or red chlorophylls (chls) is nearly universal in this core antenna, and these red chls are known to extend the light harvesting capacity and control the rate of energy migration in PSI. Surprisingly, the significance of the structural position of the red chls in PSI remains unknown. In this study, we introduced mutations that generate specific red sites in the PSI core antenna, consistent with those observed in natural species. Using CryoEM, we characterized the structural changes at these red sites. Using transient absorption spectroscopy, we measured the effects of red chlorophyll at specific sites on energy transfer and trapping in PSI to identify their functional significance. While one site funneled energy to the reaction center, the other slowed equilibration in the antenna. These opposing effects indicate different functions are associated with the different red chlorophyll location, reconciling previous seemingly incompatible suggestions as to their functional role.

papers.title: Generating Structural Ensembles of Disordered Proteins with Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein structures have accelerated scientific discovery. However, the leading structure-prediction models are trained primarily on crystal structures, limiting their ability to sample the conformations of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can probe the diversity of IDP conformational ensembles, but these simulations are slow and costly. Leveraging the speed of generative models and the accuracy of MD, we develop Zephyr, an SE(3) equivariant diffusion model trained on simulated IDP ensembles. The model generates the structure of a single protein sequence in two phases: a coarse-grained structure is first sampled and heavy atoms are subsequently denoised onto this structure. We evaluate our method on two fronts: ensemble accuracy and sampling efficiency. Across five test systems, the model reproduces key geometric and energetic metrics of the MD ensembles, while sampling at least 63 times faster.

papers.title: A Nanomechanical Fingerprint of Centromeric Methylation Co-Localization in TNBC Chromosomal Instability
papers.abstract: Centromeric heterochromatin is maintained by a self-reinforcing loop between DNA methylation (5mC) and histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), yet whether this coupling is preserved at the level of individual chromosomes in cancer has been inaccessible to conventional epigenomic assays, which average signals across cell populations and cannot resolve single-chromosome heterogeneity. Here, we use antibody-functionalized atomic force spectroscopy to simultaneously map 5mC and H3K9me3 at the centromeres of individual metaphase chromosomes from non-tumorigenic, luminal, and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell models. Co-localized 5mC/H3K9me3 sites are mechanically stiffer than sites carrying either mark alone across the panel, revealing a cooperative biophysical signature of epigenetic crosstalk. Luminal chromosomes acquire the highest mark density, co-localization, and stiffness, whereas TNBC chromosomes show reduced density and diminished, though not absent, co-localization and stiffness, converging toward the low baseline of non-tumorigenic epithelium. TGF-{beta}1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition reproduces this attenuated phenotype in luminal cells, linking it directly to a process central to TNBC aggressiveness. These biophysical parameters classify cancer versus non-tumorigenic chromosomes with near-perfect, cross-validated accuracy, and further resolve the two TNBC subtypes using colocalization-derived features alone (macro-F1 = 0.933). These results establish the mechanical consequence of epigenetic mark co-localization as a single-chromosome-resolvable signature of centromeric organization, attenuated in aggressive breast cancer, and demonstrate a force-spectroscopy platform for mechano-epigenetic profiling of cancer chromosomes.

papers.title: Plunge freezing tweezers with ultrasonic excitation for reducing preferred particle orientation in cryo-EM
papers.abstract: Preferred particle orientation, which results from the adsorption of proteins to the air-water interface, is a frequently encountered issue in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Particles then present only a limited number of views, which are oversampled during data acquisition at the expense of throughput, while other views may be missing altogether. In severe cases, a high-resolution reconstruction becomes unattainable. We have recently established that ultrasonic excitation of the sample during vitrification improves the angular distribution by detaching particles from the air-water interface and reshuffling their orientations. Here, we describe an implementation of this principle for a plunge freezing apparatus, in which the ultrasonic transducer is integrated into the head of the pair of tweezers holding the sample, and show that this design is able to reduce preferred orientation. We demonstrate this for hemagglutinin, the canonical example of preferred orientation, and show that the fraction of side and tilted views increases with the excitation amplitude. This allows us to obtain a complete reconstruction of the trimer at 2.5 [A].

papers.title: Complex folding kinetics of multi-domain proteins disentangled with periodic forces by magnetic tweezers
papers.abstract: Force spectroscopy enables direct investigation of the interplay between free energy and transition kinetics in proteins and nucleic acids. However, multi-domain proteins often display multiple intermediate structures with diverse stabilities and kinetics, making equilibrium conditions difficult to achieve and out-of-equilibrium experiments challenging to interpret. We introduce a single-molecule force spectroscopy assay using periodic forces and high-resolution magnetic tweezers to bridge different stabilities, selectively enhance intermediate populations, and rigorously analyze multi-domain protein folding kinetics at quasi-equilibrium. By applying well-defined periodic square force functions with tunable steady states, we first validate our framework on the two-state folder {lambda}6-85, demonstrating that periodic force experiments can reproduce equilibrium kinetics. Extending this approach to the multi-domain protein mimic (Protein L), we show that tuning force, frequency, and amplitude enhances populations of distinct intermediate states. Finally, we dissect the entangled states of the hybrid two-domain protein {lambda}-L, where a 100-fold difference in domain kinetics precludes equilibrium analysis, by expanding from a two-state to a three-state periodic force protocol to direct intermediate populations. Our assay and analysis framework open new possibilities for deciphering complex multi-domain folds and their multi-dimensional folding pathways.

papers.title: Conformational dynamics of ND2 antiporter-like subunit in intact and truncated complex I
papers.abstract: Respiratory complex I is a large redox-driven proton pump and contributes to the proton motive force required for ATP generation in mitochondria and bacteria. It has been extensively studied with structural and biochemical approaches leading to enhanced understanding of its three- dimensional architecture. Despite significant progress in deciphering its catalytic function, the redox-coupled proton pumping mechanism remains unclear and extensively debated. The three membrane-bound antiporter-like subunits ND2, ND4 and ND5 are responsible for pumping protons from the negatively charged side (N-side) of the membrane to the positively charged side (P-side). Emerging evidence supports the role of ND5 subunit in releasing pumped protons to the P-side of the membrane, but the question whether ND2 and ND4 also contribute to proton release remains unanswered. Here, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of an intact and a truncated model of complex I in which ND5 and ND4 subunits are removed in-silico. The simulation data reveals a previously unobserved conformational change in the P-side region of ND2 subunit that occurs much more easily in a truncated model of complex I, as also estimated based on free energy calculations. The conformational change, in part triggered by the artificial exposure of ND2 subunit to lipid bilayer, results in a local hydration of the region, similar to what has been observed in recent cryo-EM structure of plant CI:CIII2 supercomplex. We discuss the functional relevance of observed conformational transitions and identify residues that can be manipulated with biochemical approaches to shed light on proton pumping by complex I.

papers.title: Integrating cell-state and enhancer constraints discriminates models of PU.1 regulation during hematopoietic differentiation
papers.abstract: Distinct PU.1 levels are associated with progenitor, B-cell, and macrophage states during hematopoietic differentiation. A previous dynamical-systems model attributed these levels to multistability generated by PU.1 autoregulation coupled to feedback between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle progression, but its predictions were not quantitatively evaluated against the motivating measurements. Here, we test this mechanism using reported measurements of PU.1 abundance, its synthesis rate, and cell-cycle duration, and develop progressively more mechanistic alternatives. The original growth-feedback model neither represents the two reported progenitor groups nor reproduces the nonmonotonic relationship between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle length. Even with experimentally measured cell-type-specific growth rates, PU.1 autoregulation alone does not reproduce the observed PU.1 abundance and synthesis rates across cell states. Reproducing the cell-state measurements requires an additional cell-state-dependent input to PU.1 production. Guided by enhancer regulation, we model positive feedback between PU.1 and C/EBP and constrain it with reporter measurements, but this architecture cannot jointly reproduce the reporter and cell-state datasets. Adding RUNX1 permits data-consistent stable states when high effective cooperativity in PU.1-dependent C/EBP activation is allowed. Thus, combined dynamical and cis-regulatory constraints support additional regulation of PU.1 production beyond autoregulation, cell-type-specific dilution, and C/EBP feedback. The RUNX1-extended architecture provides one biologically grounded realization and generates experimentally testable hypotheses for differentiation networks.

papers.title: Gag proteolysis drives HIV-1 envelope conformational closure through the gp41 cytoplasmic tail
papers.abstract: HIV-1 must present a fusion-competent envelope glycoprotein (Env) to enter host cells while concealing the very conformation targeted by broadly neutralising antibodies (bnAbs). How the virus resolves this conflict has remained unclear. Using a minimally invasive nanobody-labelling strategy targeting Env's V4 loop, we combine single-virus FRET, fluorescence lifetime cross-correlation spectroscopy, and DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy to resolve Env conformation on individual, intact virions from the primary isolate JR-FL. We show that immature virions predominantly display an open Env conformation, while Gag maturation drives acquisition of the tightly closed, fusion-competent State 1 that harbours the principal bnAb epitope. Truncating the Env cytoplasmic tail abolishes this regulation, identifying the gp41 tail as the conduit linking Gag lattice maturation to Env's conformational fate. We further show that bnAb b12 preferentially binds open Env on immature virions, supporting a decoy mechanism that shields mature virions from immune recognition, with direct implications for HIV-1 vaccine design.

papers.title: Structural basis of selective phospholipid recognition and local membrane deformation by CTL1
papers.abstract: The physiological function of the human choline transporter-like protein CTL1 (SLC44A1) remains elusive despite its implication in key pathophysiological processes. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, native mass spectrometry, lipidomics, molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays to characterise the molecular basis of phospholipid recognition by CTL1 and explore its potential molecular role. High-resolution structures of CTL1 in both monomeric and dimeric states reveal a broad amphipathic cavity and an extracellular domain that accommodate multiple phospholipid species, identifying phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidic acid as endogenous CTL1 ligands. Molecular dynamics simulations show spontaneous phospholipid recruitment into these conserved binding sites accompanied by membrane thinning, curvature and local phospholipid reorganisation, with membrane deformation being enhanced upon dimerisation. Functional analyses in mammalian cells and in reconstituted proteoliposomes failed to detect CTL1-mediated choline transport, supporting a function distinct from canonical choline uptake. Together, our findings suggest that CTL1 acts as a phospholipid-binding protein capable of locally deforming the membrane and provide a structural framework linking phospholipid recognition to membrane organisation. These results offer new insights into potential mechanisms underlying the altered phospholipid homeostasis associated with CTL1 dysfunction in neurological diseases and cancer.

papers.title: Shear Strain Stiffening in Cartilage is Governed by a Mechanical Phase Transition
papers.abstract: Large shear deformation in cartilage can lead to tissue failure and injury, which are often precursors to diseases such as post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Under shear, cartilage strain-stiffens prior to failure, which makes stiffening an important indicator of changes to the loading of the extracellular matrix that gives rise to this tissue's properties. While a variety of stiffening mechanisms ranging from uncrimping to fiber-alignment have been explored, whether such mechanisms apply to the depth dependent shear strain stiffening in articular cartilage remains poorly understood. Here, we present experiments and theory that support the idea that the strain-stiffening behavior is caused by a mechanical phase transition from a random isotropic network whose mechanics arise primarily from bending-dominated modes to one where the mechanics arise from stretching-dominated modes. Indeed, consistent with network model predictions, we find that stress-strain data for all depths can be collapsed onto a single universal curve that diverges at a depth-dependent critical strain. These results show that increasing the local concentration of collagen, which constitutes the primary load-bearing network in cartilage, decreases the critical strain at which the strain-stiffening transition occurs, while increasing the low-strain elastic modulus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that bulk compression leads to a higher critical strain and decreased low-strain elastic modulus. Network simulations capture this rich behavior, and indicate that under compression the network collapses, which allows for larger strains before the transition from bending-dominated to stretching-dominated mechanics occurs. Collectively, these findings shed light on the roles that tissue composition and axial strain play in the mechanisms that organize how articular cartilage stiffens during the lead-up to injury.

papers.title: Cellular Density Homeostasis Is Governed by an Anisotropic Attractor and Predictive Feedback Control
papers.abstract: Cell density is a fundamental biophysical property of living cells, yet the dynamical architecture underlying density homeostasis remains unknown. Here, we reconstruct the geometry, dynamics, and control structure governing cellular density regulation from single-cell mass-volume measurements acquired during recovery from osmotic perturbation. We identify a persistent anisotropic attractor in mass-volume state space that permits coordinated density-preserving fluctuations while strongly suppressing density-changing deviations. Optimal transport analysis reveals directed recovery trajectories confined to this attractor, enabling inference of an effective density-restoring control law. Density deviations are associated with coordinated changes in biomass accumulation and volume expansion that together generate an effective density-restoring control law. Moreover, density error contains significant predictive information regarding future corrective behavior, revealing an information-rich component of cellular regulation. Together, these findings establish cellular density homeostasis as an emergent dynamical control process and demonstrate how attractor reconstruction, optimal transport, and information theory can be combined to uncover the organizing principles of biological homeostasis.

papers.title: Interplay of mechanics, growth and viral infection dynamics in a spatially expanding bacterial colony
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of the spread of the infection due to a phage- during the range expansion of an E coli colony. We find a rich panoply of spatio-temporal dynamics at large colony-level length scales, arising due to the interplay of mechanical forces, growth and viral infection dynamics at smaller cellular length scales. Strikingly, the phages "surf" the front of the growing bacterial colony by hitchhiking on E coli that are advected due to the growth of bacteria in the colony, resulting in an anisotropic spread of the phages. We identify microscopic processes - of the phage release during lysis (occurring on short millisecond timescales at length scales close to that of a single bacterium) and local nematic alignment of the rod-like E coli bacteria (occurring on timescales comparable to the bacterial growth rate and the length scales of a few bacterial cells) - that enhance the advective effects driving the hitchhiking behavior. Combining our experiments with a mathematical model, we explain the multiple spatio-temporal dynamical regimes - from the coexistence of uninfected bacteria, resistant (lysogenic) cells and phages, to fixed points where the entire population turns resistant or remains uninfected. Our work broaches a new frontier in the investigation of eco-evolutionary processes arising from the mechanical and ecological forces due to the interactions between viruses and their hosts.

papers.title: Mechanical regulation of endocytosis by protein droplet capillary forces
papers.abstract: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) is the primary pathway for internalization of extracellular and membrane cargo in eukaryotic cells. It is characterized by a patch of the plasma membrane invaginating and pinching off to generate a cytoplasmic vesicle. Recently, experimental evidence has begun to accumulate in support of proteins assembling into liquid-like condensates at nascent CME sites, but potential functional consequences are not understood. Given that condensate capillary forces can influence membrane bending, we constructed complementary analytical and numerical model systems to probe the mechanical influence of a protein droplet on endocytosis. Model evaluations and analysis reveal that a droplet can regulate the progression of endocytosis by stalling invagination until the droplet grows past a threshold size. After the droplet-mediated brake is released, the droplet provides a force that can drive the membrane bud toward scission. Thus, we propose a ``mechanical timer'' mechanism as a function for protein phase separation in cellular membrane trafficking.

papers.title: e^-2 Threshold for Bistability in Non-equilibrium Sorting of Biomolecular Condensates
papers.abstract: Cells use ATP-driven chaperones to extract clients from biomolecular condensates selectively, yet no closed-form criterion links molecular parameters to condensate quality control. We derive a minimal non-equilibrium sorting reactor model that reduces the reaction-diffusion dynamics to one algebraic equation. In the idealized low-load limit, a concentration-dependent partition coefficient produces a saddle-node bifurcation between functional clearance and pathological storage. The critical Damk"ohler number is (mathrm{Da}_{0c}=e^{-2}) and is independent of the feedback strength. Corrections shift the value but preserve the topology. The model predicts a Kramers-type functional lifetime and recovery costs that scale as (R^3). Critical slowing down near the bifurcation provides early-warning signatures for FCS and FRAP.

papers.title: Methylglyoxal-derived glycation tunes nuclear viscoelasticity
papers.abstract: Reactive carbonyl metabolites such as methylglyoxal (MGO) accumulate in diabetes, aging, and metabolic disease, conditions frequently associated with pathological stiffening of human cells and tissues. While glycation of extracellular matrices and cytoskeletal proteins is known to contribute to these mechanical changes, whether the nucleus itself is a direct mechanical target of carbonyl stress remains unknown. Here, by combining advanced atomic force microscopy-based nanomechanical probing with correlative confocal imaging, we show that MGO-derived glycation directly remodels isolated cell nuclei, increasing stiffness, reducing fluidity, and restricting intranuclear deformation propagation. MGO-derived adducts accumulate prominently at the nuclear envelope, and perturbation of lamin A/C and chromatin state reveals that both structures contribute to glycation-induced stiffening. In cells, chronic MGO exposure induces nucleus-intrinsic stiffening and biases YAP nuclear localization in a substrate-stiffness-dependent manner, linking nuclear glycation to altered mechanosensitive regulation. In vivo, cardiac nuclear stiffening is only observed along with increased immunodetected MGO-adduct burden, while nuclear fluidity remains largely preserved. Together, these findings establish nonenzymatic glycation as a metabolic mechanism that remodels nuclear mechanics and alters cellular mechanosensing, revealing a previously unrecognized physical consequence of carbonyl stress.

papers.title: Distinct Aβ40 and Aβ42 co-assembly pathways with free lipids: Experiment-driven MD study
papers.abstract: Amyloid {beta}-protein (A{beta}), which is known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD), is also involved in several physiological functions. Of the two predominant isoforms, A{beta}40 and A{beta}42, the latter is more aggregation-prone and more active in health and disease. In the brain, A{beta} interacts with free lipids, which may affect its assembly pathways. Here, thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence spectroscopy is combined with molecular dynamics (MD) to investigate A{beta}40 and A{beta}42 co-assembly with free dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) and DMPC/cholesterol (CHOL) lipids. ThT measurements at several protein-to-lipid (PL) ratios show isoform- and lipid composition-dependent kinetics of A{beta} fibril formation with clear isoform-dependent lipid effects at a PL ratio of 1:5. Early co-assembly stages of six A{beta}40/A{beta}42 with DMPC and DMPC/CHOL lipids at this PL ratio are then examined by MD. MD results indicate that lipids alter the secondary structure more and interact more avidly with A{beta}40 than with A{beta}42. In turn, A{beta}40 increases the planar order of lipid bicelles more than A{beta}42. Unlike A{beta}40, A{beta}42 decreases the nematic order of CHOL. In DMPC/CHOL lipids, A{beta}42 but not A{beta}40 exhibits two A{beta}-lipid interaction modes associated with mutually exclusive A{beta}42-lipid and A{beta}42-A{beta}42 interactions. Our MD findings provide a plausible explanation for an experimentally observed increase in the lag time for A{beta}40 fibril formation in DMPC lipids and even more so in DMPC/CHOL lipids that contrasts with much smaller effects of lipids on A{beta}42 fibril formation and offer additional atomistic-level insights into A{beta} co-assembly with lipids amenable to experimental testing.

papers.title: Dendritic Morphology Constrains Microtubule Dynamics and Organization
papers.abstract: Neuronal dendrites form highly branched morphologies supported by spatially patterned microtubule arrays that are essential for intracellular transport and structural stability, yet how this organization is established and maintained remains unclear. Here we analyze microtubule behavior in Drosophila sensory neurons using live-cell imaging, deep learning-based analysis, and genetic perturbations. We find that microtubules are shorter and fewer in thin distal branches and progressively longer and more abundant in thicker proximal branches. Locally, polymerization slows in narrow branches due to soluble tubulin depletion, while catastrophe frequency increases near branch points upon cortical encounter. A physical model incorporating these morphology-dependent constraints reproduces both local microtubule dynamics and global organization. Inverting the textbook view that microtubule dynamics shape cell morphology, our results demonstrate that, on short timescales, cell morphology instead constrains microtubule dynamics, thereby determining large-scale cytoskeletal organization.

papers.title: Curvature sensing and generation by diverse membrane-tethered polymers can be explained by a unifying physical model
papers.abstract: Cell membranes are decorated by dense, polymeric macromolecules such as proteins with bulky intrinsically disordered regions, glycosylated proteins, and glycopolymers. Experiments have illustrated that the curvature of cellular membranes, which plays a role in diverse biological processes, can be regulated by the local density of these membrane-tethered polymers and their response to environmental changes. However, the mechanisms underlying the feedback between solution conditions, membrane curvature, and the local density and molecular weight of membrane-tethered polymers remain largely unexplored. In this work, using a combination of theory and experiment, we show that the ionic strength of the surrounding solution and the degree of ionization both play important roles in regulating the conformation of the membrane-tethered polymers, which in turn influences their membrane curvature generation capabilities. Specifically, we show that for negatively charged, disordered proteins and glycans, the thickness of the polymer brush decreases with ionic strength but increases with grafting density and degree of ionization, resulting in enhanced sensitivity to membrane curvature and an amplified ability to drive membrane curvature at lower ionic concentrations. Our findings reveal a mechanism by which membrane-tethered polymers generate membrane curvature to minimize free energy, with the extent of curvature generation modulated by the polymer grafting density and layer thickness, as well as by the ionic strength of the surrounding solution. The implications of these findings are broad, suggesting that perturbations to biopolymer charge, such as sialylation of glycans and phosphorylation of disordered proteins, could actively modulate membrane curvature induction in diverse cellular processes from endocytosis to cell motility.

papers.title: Measuring protein conformational changes with genetically encoded bipyridylalanine and transition-metal ion FRET
papers.abstract: Transition-metal ion Forster resonance energy transfer (tmFRET) measures short-range distances and conformational changes in proteins, but its distance sensitivity depends on the donor-acceptor pair. Here, we establish the metal-chelating noncanonical amino acid bipyridylalanine (bpyA) as a flexible, genetically encoded acceptor platform whose Forster distance (R0) can be tuned without changing protein labeling. Cu2+, Cu2+ complexed with nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA), and Fe2+ form distinct acceptors at the same bpyA site, allowing distance sensitivity to be adjusted by changing the solution conditions. We incorporated bpyA at two sites in maltose binding protein (MBP) and labeled nearby engineered cysteines with the donor fluorophore BODIPY. The resulting [Cu(bpyA)]2+, [CuNTA(bpyA)]2+, and [Fe(bpyA)]2+ acceptors provided R0 values ranging from 13.9 to 21.2 [A]. Analysis of time-resolved tmFRET data recovered donor-acceptor distance distributions and maltose-dependent changes consistent with structural predictions. At the 237/295 site pair, both copper and iron acceptors resolved the maltose-dependent decrease in distance. At the 309/322 site pair, [Cu(bpyA)]2+ did not appreciably resolve the distance increase, whereas adding NTA shifted R0 toward shorter distances and enabled detection of an increase from 12.1 to 14.4 [A]. These results demonstrate that a single bpyA-labeled protein preparation supports multiple tmFRET acceptors, providing a cysteine-independent acceptor-labeling strategy with adjustable distance sensitivity.
